hero.headline: Fort Pierce manufactured home owners can now access $167 million in Florida storm repair funding
hero.body:
Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect on July 1st, and one of them could significantly help some of the state's most vulnerable homeowners. Senate Bill 594 opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to assist mobile and manufactured home owners with emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change came in response to an investigation that revealed nearly 700,000 manufactured homes across Florida, about two-thirds of the state's total, were built before current federal safety standards and cannot withstand modern storms.

The push for this funding began after an EF-3 tornado destroyed the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce. The disaster obliterated 138 homes and killed six residents. Paula Richards, a Spanish Lakes resident, received repair estimates ranging from $10,000 to $15,000 but could not afford the costs. Many seniors living in older manufactured homes across Florida face the same financial barriers to making their structures safer. Their pleas for assistance eventually reached lawmakers, who responded by passing Senate Bill 594 in spring 2026.

Implementation of the program varies by county. Martin County Human Services reports that an online portal will open in August, with about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, now available to eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. St. Lucie County is still waiting for final guidance from the state before announcing its application process. Indian River County officials will present the legislative change to their Board on August 18th, with a September 30th deadline to submit their implementation plan to the state. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plans to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance once the program opens.

People interested in applying should visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website to check income eligibility and learn how to apply. Applications can be submitted online or by mail. According to Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services, the funding operates on a first-come, first-served basis, making it important for residents to gather their paperwork quickly. While counties generally follow the same timeframe based on a calendar from the Florida Housing Coalition, the specific timeline varies by location. Beginning preparation now by visiting the state website and selecting your county will help you understand what funding is available and who to contact when applications open in your area.

cards.headline: DeSantis moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa as terrorist organizations under new Florida law
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa, and several car.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa, Tren de Aragua, Sinaloa-related groups, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as terrorist organizations under HB 1471, a new state law that took effect July 1. At a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, DeSantis said the state is preparing its first slate of designations under the law, formally titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations." The law authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend designations, which must be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote before taking effect. Designated organizations can face public-funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support. DeSantis said the designations would affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school-choice scholarship program.

DeSantis framed the announcement as a continuation of a December executive order targeting CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood that directed state agencies to deny contracts, funding and other public benefits to those providing support to the groups. That order was quickly challenged in federal court and temporarily blocked in March after CAIR, CAIR Florida and civil-rights groups sued, arguing it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law gives the state better legal footing. The designations are not final until the Cabinet signs off. Attorneys representing CAIR said they expect another court fight, with Scott McCoy, deputy legal director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, stating the U.S. Constitution is supreme in Florida.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents hit with thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.teaser: Homeowners along Franwood Drive in unincorporated Palm Beach County received notices from Delray Beach demanding back payments for up to three years of sewer fees, with some bills exceeding $4,000.
cards.body:
Homeowners in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood are facing unexpected bills for years of unpaid sewer fees after the city of Delray Beach completed an audit in April 2026. Several residents along Franwood Drive received notices demanding retroactive payments, with some bills exceeding $4,000. The notices cover up to three years of charges and establish new monthly sewer fees moving forward. Candace Etzler received a bill for $3,139, and she estimates that at least a dozen homeowners in her neighborhood received similar notices. Resident Ruth Stephens was charged $4,494.92 and expressed her concern about the unexpected expense. Both homeowners said they fear their sewer service could be disconnected if they fail to pay the retroactive charges.

The billing stems from events dating back to 1998, when nearby development disrupted the neighborhood's septic systems. Florida state law required residents to connect to the closest municipal sewer system following the disruption. Etzler explained the situation, saying "They shook up our drain fields for our septic and the state law mandates you to hook up to the municipality that's closest to you." According to residents, they previously attempted to pay for sewer service but were told by the city that payment was not required. This confusion appears to have created the gap between when they should have begun paying and when the city actually billed them for the service.

Residents are questioning how the city calculated the retroactive charges. Etzler challenged the methodology, asking "How can you have this random number of 36 months and at the price of $90 a month." Stephens echoed the frustration, stating "I understand having to pay a monthly fee, but my total was $4,494.92, and that's hard for people to just come up with." Some residents have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans out of concern about potential disconnection.

City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the billing in a statement, explaining "When a sewer connection is identified, the City's responsibility is to determine what costs were incurred and recover the applicable fees. This is about ensuring that public utility costs are paid by those receiving the service rather than being shifted to the taxpayers." County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has contacted the county attorney's office to investigate the legality of both the retroactive charges and the monthly payment requirements going forward. The situation highlights a dispute over municipal billing practices and whether residents should bear the full cost of utility services they were unable to pay earlier.

cards.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks, pool party at North Palm Beach Country Club

Starting at 4:30 p.m., families can participate in lawn games and activities including cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga, face painting and other yard games. The Clubhouse will begin serving a Fourth of July barbecue buffet at the same time, allowing families to gather for dinner. Live music from the band Solstice Reign is scheduled to start around 6 p.m., providing entertainment as the sun sets and the evening progresses toward the fireworks finale.

According to Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, the golf course will offer one of the best vantage points for viewing the fireworks display. Whether visitors choose to watch from the golf course, the pool area or the lawn, the venue provides multiple locations to enjoy the evening's entertainment. The event combines dining, recreation and entertainment into a comprehensive celebration designed for all ages and interests.

cards.headline: TikTok, Google ignore Florida child social media safety law while Meta complies
cards.teaser: Most major tech companies are not complying with Florida's landmark social media law banning children under 14 from creating accounts, despite the law taking effect after a federal appeals court cleared it in November.
cards.body:
After nearly two years of legal battles with Big Tech trade associations, Florida's landmark social media law finally took effect following an 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling in November. However, most major technology companies covered under the law are not complying with its requirements. HB 3, which bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for those aged 14 and 15, passed the Legislature in March 2024 and was signed by Governor Ron DeSantis that same month. The legislation was a signature priority for then-House Speaker Paul Renner, who emphasized at the bill signing that developing brains are vulnerable to addictive technologies.

Attorney General James Uthmeier has pursued aggressive enforcement since the law survived court challenges. He announced that Meta has complied with HB 3 by suspending hundreds of thousands of underage accounts and confirmed the company would implement compliance measures by early May. However, TikTok and Google, which owns YouTube and YouTube Kids, have remained silent on their compliance plans and effectively ignored the law. Uthmeier warned noncompliant platforms face $50,000-per-violation fines that could accumulate into billions of dollars. In June, he sued TikTok for violating HB 3 by allowing underage accounts to persist and failing to secure proper parental consent for older teenagers, stating that TikTok knowingly deceives parents and exposes children to harmful content.

Google's continued silence is particularly significant given YouTube's massive presence in young people's lives. Research from Pew shows that roughly nine in 10 U.S. teenagers use YouTube, more than any other platform, with approximately three-quarters using it daily. The exposure risks are substantial: 46 percent of parents with children age 11 or younger reported their child encountered inappropriate content on YouTube. Even YouTube Kids, marketed for children as young as 4, has been found serving content addressing gender ideology and systemic racism, according to congressional testimony cited by Fox News. These are topics that DeSantis and Uthmeier have both criticized extensively.

At a press conference, Uthmeier directly addressed tech platforms still resisting compliance. "YouTube and others, you got to wake up. This is real and you can save lives," he said. Whether Google, TikTok, Roblox and other platforms will follow Meta's compliance remains uncertain. If holdouts persist in noncompliance, Uthmeier indicated they will face significant financial consequences and urged them to "open up your checkbook."

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: West Palm Beach secured $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue, one of the city's most flood-prone roads.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach residents dealing with chronic flooding on Australian Avenue will finally see relief after Gov. Ron DeSantis signed $2 million in state funding for drainage improvements into the new Florida budget Monday. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area residents say has flooded for decades, even during light rainstorms. State Sen. Mack Bernard called securing the funding a major step forward after DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said flooding has affected his daily routine since childhood, forcing him to ride his bike through underwater streets. Marion Hawkins, another nearby resident, calls the area "Lake Australian Avenue" and said rainwater reaches her driveway and leaves debris scattered across her property after storms.

The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. Palm Beach County Public Works Director David Ricks presented improvement plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to accommodate larger underground drainage pipes. According to county documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029. Vanriel said the improvements cannot come soon enough for a neighborhood that needs an upgrade.

cards.headline: Palm Beach International Airport name change to Donald J. Trump International takes effect July 9
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport is becoming Donald J. Trump International Airport on July 9, with signage changes already underway at a cost of $2.75 million funded by the state of Florida.
cards.body:
Palm Beach International Airport's official name change to Donald J. Trump International Airport takes effect July 9. The three-letter designation will shift from PBI to DJT for airline reservations and navigation purposes, with that transition expected in August. The airport remains owned by Palm Beach County, though Trump owns the trademark on the new name. Sign changes are being funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million and are already underway throughout the airport, though passengers continue departing and arriving as usual.

Airport officials said nothing should change for passengers beyond the signage. The airport posted a statement on its website acknowledging that the required name change may be received in different ways by passengers. Two lawsuits are attempting to stop the name change. George Poncy, one of the plaintiffs suing to block it, said the state seems to be stalling and delaying any hearing before a judge. Sign changes will happen gradually, meaning passengers will likely notice the transition as it unfolds.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: Harper Aberman of Jensen Beach will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend after years of competitive sailing that began at a Pennsylvania summer camp.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend. Her sailing journey began at age four when her grandparents enrolled her in a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania. After attending for eight weeks, Aberman's passion for the sport solidified. When her family moved to Jensen Beach, she joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive career took shape.

Aberman has won countless tournaments and placed in several national competitions, establishing herself as one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. She describes herself as an adrenaline junkie, drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. She received news of her Team USA selection during Spring Break via email. Aberman has spent the past few weeks training in Spain before the competition, with racing set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz one year later: Everglades detention facility closed after billion-dollar cost
cards.teaser: One year after Florida opened the controversial Alligator Alcatraz immigration detention facility in the Everglades, the camp has closed, leaving questions about more than $1 billion spent by Florida taxpayers.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis opened Alligator Alcatraz on July 1, 2025, marking the first time a state had run a detention facility exclusively for immigration detainees. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County, then used emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to build the facility in eight days. Trump said FEMA would pay for the facility. Using ICE data, approximately 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims that only dangerous migrants would be housed there.

Immigration attorneys and detainees raised alarms about conditions inside. The ACLU filed a federal lawsuit over detainees' access to legal counsel, while Friends of the Everglades, the Miccosukee Tribe, and environmental groups sued claiming the construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. A district court judge issued a preliminary injunction in August ordering dismantling of the facility, but an appeals court reversed that decision in September. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover costs exceeding $1 billion. ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman rallies for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes kill relatives
cards.teaser: Alessandra De La Correa spent six hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, collapsing buildings and killing members of her family.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering if her parents survived two devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night after the quake struck. De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, a volleyball player, had been rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. Her parents survived, but the earthquake destroyed their home and businesses in La Guaira, including her mother's children's clothing store that was located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Her uncle's apartment building also collapsed moments before he entered it.

Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign to support De La Correa's relatives, aiming to raise $15,000. De La Correa said her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings. They managed to recover some clothing, photos and documents, but her uncle could not recover even one fork from his apartment. De La Correa's parents, now over 60, had also lost nearly everything in another deadly disaster in the same region in the 1990s and must start again.

hero.headline: Martin County free clinic sees surge in patients after federal health subsidies expired
hero.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is treating more patients after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired at the start of this year, leaving many low-income residents without health insurance.
hero.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free medical clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is experiencing increased patient demand following the expiration of enhanced financial assistance programs through the Affordable Care Act at the start of the year. The clinic's leadership says the loss of these federal subsidies has left many residents without health insurance and unable to access medical care. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, the clinic's medical director, reports that more than 200,000 people across Florida did not renew their ACA coverage this year, with estimates suggesting upwards of 500 Martin County residents lost their insurance access as a result of the subsidy expiration.

One patient affected by the change is Rokaya McGarry, who could no longer afford health insurance premiums after the enhanced subsidies ended. She initially worried about her health situation, knowing that without insurance, emergency rooms would be her only option for care. McGarry said, "Panic set in because you know that the only way that you're going to be helped as far as health is to go to an Emergency." Her situation became urgent when she fell ill following the loss of her mother, experiencing weakness and bronchitis. "The grief and the everything I had like a bronchitis I felt very weak and in a moment of desperation," McGarry said. She contacted Volunteers in Medicine and received care within a day.

According to Bromberg, the loss of insurance coverage poses serious health risks for people who delay seeking preventive care. "There are a lot of things that get screened for that if they're found early can prevent terrible outcomes," he explained. While only about 20 patients have sought care at the clinic specifically after losing ACA coverage, Bromberg believes many more Martin County residents are in similar situations. He emphasized the clinic's capacity to help, stating, "There are so many more out there that can come and see us. We have the capacity for more."

The clinic provides free medical care without restrictions to individuals earning under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. McGarry expressed deep gratitude for the care she received, saying, "I can't even express how grateful I am to them because I don't know where I'd be." As the clinic continues to serve patients who lost coverage, its leadership encourages others in similar circumstances to reach out for assistance.

cards.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection opens July 6 at Historical Society of Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will go on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting July 6, with free admission through August.
cards.body:
One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will open July 6 at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach. Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns the collection with his brother, and they are displaying it to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The exhibit, titled Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon, features over 50 books written by, printed by or about Franklin, along with work from his time as a printer. More than 120 pieces are on display in total.

Highlights include a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's Philadelphia home, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," and original medallions made when Franklin was representing France during the American Revolution. The exhibit also features a plaster model for the Libertas Americana medal designed by Franklin, and the glass armonica, which Franklin called his favorite invention. Jacobson's stepfather started the collection 50 years ago. Jacobson and his brother eventually bought the remains of the collection and continued it for 15 years. The exhibit is free to the public and runs through August at 300 N Dixie Highway.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach receives $2 million in state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue, a roadway that has flooded for years.
cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. State Sen. Mack Bernard said securing the funding was a major step forward after previous setbacks, noting the governor vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost.

Residents along the roadway have dealt with persistent flooding even during routine rain. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the corridor, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue" because water comes up to her driveway and leaves debris scattered across her property after storms. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented improvement plans three years ago that would create a larger median and expand road and shoulder areas to accommodate larger underground drainage pipes. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

cards.headline: Florida opens $167 million in state funding for manufactured home repairs starting August 1
cards.teaser: Senate Bill 594 opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1, opening $167 million in state SHIP funding to help mobile and manufactured homeowners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law followed an investigation that exposed nearly 700,000 Florida mobile and manufactured homes built before current federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms. The change was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that destroyed 138 homes at Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce and killed six residents.

Martin County Human Services will open an online portal in August for eligible applicants. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, will be available for manufactured homeowners. Applicants can complete an online application or call the office to request one by mail. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance once the program opens. St. Lucie County is awaiting final state guidance before announcing its application process. Indian River County will present the legislative change to its Board on August 18, with a September 30 deadline to submit its plan to the state. All funding is first come, first served.

cards.headline: One year later: Alligator Alcatraz detention facility closed after costing Florida over $1 billion
cards.teaser: The controversial immigration detention facility known as Alligator Alcatraz, which opened in the Everglades on July 1, 2025, closed in June after costing Florida taxpayers over $1 billion.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced the opening of Alligator Alcatraz alongside Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis one year ago. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County, then used emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to build the facility in eight days. Trump said FEMA would pay for the facility, but a $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover the costs. Most estimates put the total price tag at more than $1 billion.

Using ICE's own data, about 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, debunking government claims that only criminals would be sent there. Immigration attorney Eric Lee said the conditions were the worst he had experienced in over a decade of practice. A district court judge sided with environmental groups led by Friends of the Everglades Director Eve Samples in August, issuing a preliminary injunction to dismantle the facility, but an appeals court reversed that decision in September. ICE confirmed in June that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through Alligator Alcatraz. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
hero.body:
A Jensen Beach teenager will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend, marking the culmination of years spent competing in one of sailing's most prestigious youth circuits. Harper Aberman's journey in the sport began at age four when her grandparents enrolled her in a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania. While her cousin disliked the experience, Aberman embraced sailing immediately. "I fell in love with it, and I ended up going for eight weeks," she said of those early summers.

When Aberman's family relocated to Jensen Beach, she joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career truly accelerated. "That is where the sailing adventure took off for me," Aberman recalled. She has since become one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit, winning countless tournaments and placing in several national competitions. Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie, drawn to sailing's most demanding conditions. She acknowledges the physical challenges of competitive racing, noting that windy conditions have historically caused her to struggle with staying upright and avoiding the water.

The opportunity to compete for Team USA arrived unexpectedly during Spring Break when Aberman received an email confirming her selection. The moment sparked excitement throughout her household. "I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer,'" she said of learning the news. The family's summer plans transformed instantly from routine to extraordinary with the prospect of traveling to France for the international competition.

In preparation for the championship, Aberman has spent the past several weeks training intensively in Spain. She emphasized the significant commitment required to compete at this level, stating that preparation has involved "a lot of recovery and a lot of time and effort out on the water." Despite the demanding training schedule, Aberman expressed confidence that the effort will prove worthwhile, particularly given the prestige of the venue hosting the championship. Racing is scheduled to begin Monday, setting the stage for Aberman to compete alongside the world's top young sailors in her division.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for emergency repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Martin County will open an online portal in August allowing mobile and manufactured home owners to apply for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits using state SHIP funding.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1st, opening $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change follows an investigation that exposed hundreds of thousands of older homes across Florida that cannot stand up to modern storms. Nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes, about two-thirds of Florida's more than 1 million such homes, were built before today's federal safety standards. The investigation began after an EF-3 tornado destroyed 138 homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, killing six people.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services says an online portal will open in August. Once it does, about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to have one mailed to them. Stellatos notes the funding is first come, first served, so getting paperwork together quickly is important. Homeowners can visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website to check income eligibility, see available funding for their area, and find contact information.

cards.headline: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County has room for more patients after ACA subsidies expired
cards.teaser: A free medical clinic in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of 2026 and says it has capacity to serve more.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, which serves low-income families in Martin County, is seeing an increase in patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of the clinic, said the expiration of the enhanced financial assistance program has left many people without health insurance and, in some cases, without access to medical care. More than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year, according to Bromberg.

Only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. Bromberg said the clinic has capacity for more patients. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached. Rokaya McGarry is one patient who could no longer afford health insurance after the enhanced subsidies expired. She said she fell very ill after losing her mother and called the clinic, which took over her care within a day.

cards.headline: Vero Beach nonprofit urgently needs box truck to deliver 100 boxes of Venezuela earthquake relief supplies
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and needs a box truck by Thursday to deliver them to Miami.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network, a Vero Beach nonprofit organization, has collected more than 100 boxes of supplies for Venezuela earthquake relief and is urgently seeking community assistance to transport them. The organization is working with Global Empowerment Mission in Miami to deliver crucial supplies to Venezuela, which is recovering from a 7.5-magnitude earthquake. Since Friday afternoon, the community response has exceeded expectations, with boxes packed with everything from diapers to medical supplies. Co-founder Juliana Marino said the organization initially thought they could transport everything in their personal cars to Miami, but there is no more room for the volume of donations.

Latinas Nexus Network is calling on the community to donate the use of a 12 to 16-foot box truck. Organizers need the truck no later than Thursday to load supplies and deliver them to Global Empowerment Mission in Miami on Friday. The cause is personal for co-founder Lourana Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and has family near the epicenter of the earthquake. Anyone who can help is asked to contact Navarro at 954-205-0700 or Marino at 772-913-0805.

cards.headline: Independence Day celebrations across Treasure Coast mark America's 250th birthday
cards.teaser: Communities across the Treasure Coast are celebrating America's 250th birthday on Saturday with fireworks, drone shows, time capsule openings and full-day events.
cards.body:
Delray Beach's Fourth of July Celebration returns to East Atlantic Avenue and A1A on Saturday, July 4, drawing more than 20,000 people to the family-friendly event that has been a tradition for over 50 years. At 5 p.m., the city will open its 1976 Bicentennial Time Capsule at the main stage at A1A. A 60-foot flag raising with the national anthem takes place at 6 p.m. at Atlantic Avenue and Seabreeze Avenue, followed by live music and entertainment from Digital Vibez. Fireworks begin at 9 p.m. All-day activities include food trucks, vendors, arts and crafts, face painting, glitter tattoos, carnival games, a photo booth, and toddler soft play.

Boca Raton's 68-year-old Independence Day tradition returns on Saturday with a full day of events celebrating America's 250th anniversary. The Firecracker 5K starts at 7:15 a.m. at Florida Atlantic University at 777 Glades Road. The Fabulous Fourth Block Party runs from 1 to 4 p.m. at Sugar Sand Park at 300 S. Military Trail, featuring kids' crafts, yard games, and a DJ. The Fabulous Finale takes place from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. at Countess de Hoernle Park at 1000 Spanish River Blvd., featuring waterfront live music and a 20-minute fireworks display at 9:10 p.m.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for Venezuelan best friend's family after deadly earthquakes
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign to support her Jensen Beach best friend's family after earthquakes in Venezuela killed several relatives and destroyed their home.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night. De La Correa's parents survived, but several relatives did not. The family lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, who had been rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when a building collapsed, her grandmother, and her uncle and his wife. The losses came just weeks after De La Correa returned from her first visit to Venezuela in several years to announce that she and her partner are expecting a baby. The earthquakes destroyed her parents' home and businesses, including her mother's children's clothing store located in a shopping mall that collapsed entirely.

Feeling powerless from abroad, Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign to support De La Correa's relatives. The campaign aims to raise $15,000 and is quickly spreading. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings. They managed to recover some clothing, photos and documents, but her uncle could not recover even one fork from his apartment.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks, pool party at North Palm Beach Country Club

Attendees can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, various games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting programs through September
cards.teaser: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer.
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. The center said guests can participate in seasonal experiences including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. According to Loggerhead Marinelife Center, the programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations during the programs may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. Loggerhead Marinelife Center said its education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: TikTok, Google ignore Florida child social media safety law while Meta complies
hero.teaser: Most major tech companies are not complying with Florida's landmark social media law banning children under 14 from creating accounts, despite the law taking effect after a federal appeals court cleared it in November.
hero.body:
After nearly two years of legal battles with Big Tech trade associations, Florida's landmark social media law finally took effect following an 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling in November. However, most major technology companies covered under the law are not complying with its requirements. HB 3, which bans children under 14 from creating social media accounts and requires parental consent for those aged 14 and 15, passed the Legislature in March 2024 and was signed by Governor Ron DeSantis that same month. The legislation was a signature priority for then-House Speaker Paul Renner, who emphasized at the bill signing that developing brains are vulnerable to addictive technologies.

Attorney General James Uthmeier has pursued aggressive enforcement since the law survived court challenges. He announced that Meta has complied with HB 3 by suspending hundreds of thousands of underage accounts and confirmed the company would implement compliance measures by early May. However, TikTok and Google, which owns YouTube and YouTube Kids, have remained silent on their compliance plans and effectively ignored the law. Uthmeier warned noncompliant platforms face $50,000-per-violation fines that could accumulate into billions of dollars. In June, he sued TikTok for violating HB 3 by allowing underage accounts to persist and failing to secure proper parental consent for older teenagers, stating that TikTok knowingly deceives parents and exposes children to harmful content.

Google's continued silence is particularly significant given YouTube's massive presence in young people's lives. Research from Pew shows that roughly nine in 10 U.S. teenagers use YouTube, more than any other platform, with approximately three-quarters using it daily. The exposure risks are substantial: 46 percent of parents with children age 11 or younger reported their child encountered inappropriate content on YouTube. Even YouTube Kids, marketed for children as young as 4, has been found serving content addressing gender ideology and systemic racism, according to congressional testimony cited by Fox News. These are topics that DeSantis and Uthmeier have both criticized extensively.

At a press conference, Uthmeier directly addressed tech platforms still resisting compliance. "YouTube and others, you got to wake up. This is real and you can save lives," he said. Whether Google, TikTok, Roblox and other platforms will follow Meta's compliance remains uncertain. If holdouts persist in noncompliance, Uthmeier indicated they will face significant financial consequences and urged them to "open up your checkbook."

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes bill to raise sovereign immunity caps, blocking first increase in 16 years
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed legislation that would have modestly raised the limits on what Floridians can receive in court settlements for government negligence without legislative approval.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed HB 145 on Wednesday, blocking the first increase in 16 years to Florida's sovereign immunity caps. The measure, sponsored by Sarasota Republican Rep. Fiona McFarland with a companion bill by Lake Mary Republican Sen. Jason Brodeur, passed with overwhelming bipartisan support in March. It would have raised caps from $200,000 per person and $300,000 per incident, last set in 2010, to $350,000 per person and $500,000 per incident. The bill also would have allowed local governments to voluntarily settle claims exceeding those caps without legislative approval. DeSantis said raising the caps would generate more unmeritorious lawsuits and that the current system effectively disincentivizes frivolous litigation.

McFarland argued the existing system creates prohibitive obstacles for people harmed by government negligence and produces vastly different outcomes depending on whether the offender was a public or private entity. More than 240 lobbyists registered to speak about the bill, many representing counties, cities and agencies facing budget shortfalls under a proposed property tax amendment on the November ballot. DeSantis countered that the current system works, noting he signed a number of claims bills this year and people have received millions of dollars. State lawmakers consider roughly a dozen claims bills annually. This year, just over a third of 14 such measures cleared both chambers.

cards.headline: DeSantis moves to designate CAIR, Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa as terrorist organizations under new Florida law
cards.teaser: Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa, and several car.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday that Florida will designate the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the Muslim Brotherhood, Antifa, Tren de Aragua, Sinaloa-related groups, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as terrorist organizations under HB 1471, a new state law that took effect July 1. At a Tampa press conference with FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass and Statewide Prosecutor Brad McVay, DeSantis said the state is preparing its first slate of designations under the law, formally titled "Systems of Law and Terrorist Organizations." The law authorizes Florida's Chief of Domestic Security to recommend designations, which must be approved or rejected by the governor and Florida Cabinet by majority vote before taking effect. Designated organizations can face public-funding restrictions, possible corporate dissolution in certain circumstances, and penalties tied to material support. DeSantis said the designations would affect state and local funding, colleges and universities, and Florida's K-12 school-choice scholarship program.

DeSantis framed the announcement as a continuation of a December executive order targeting CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood that directed state agencies to deny contracts, funding and other public benefits to those providing support to the groups. That order was quickly challenged in federal court and temporarily blocked in March after CAIR, CAIR Florida and civil-rights groups sued, arguing it violated constitutional protections. DeSantis said the new law gives the state better legal footing. The designations are not final until the Cabinet signs off. Attorneys representing CAIR said they expect another court fight, with Scott McCoy, deputy legal director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, stating the U.S. Constitution is supreme in Florida.

cards.headline: Saint Leo University and Town of St. Leo secure nearly $3 million in state budget
cards.teaser: Three budget projects totaling nearly $3 million survived Governor DeSantis' veto pen, providing funding for nursing program expansion, cybersecurity training, and stormwater infrastructure in Pasco County.
cards.body:
Saint Leo University and the Town of St. Leo secured nearly $3 million in state funding that survived Gov. Ron DeSantis' veto pen in the $117.6 billion budget he signed this week. The university received $1.2 million to expand its nursing program and $602,000 for its Cybersecurity and Cyberforensics Training and Education Center. The town received $995,000 for stormwater infrastructure supporting its proposed town center. The nursing funding addresses a statewide priority, as Florida faces a projected shortage of nearly 60,000 nurses by 2035 according to the Florida Hospital Association. Saint Leo's nursing program has grown rapidly, jumping from 77 incoming pre-nursing students in Fall 2024 to 124 in Fall 2025, with enrollment expected to top 150 this Fall. The project will reconfigure existing campus space to add three classrooms, a nursing lab, faculty offices, simulation equipment and classroom technology upgrades.

The cybersecurity investment will fund construction of a Security Operations Center and cyberforensics laboratory to help close a national talent gap that could exceed 1 million unfilled cybersecurity professionals by 2027. The funding will also support recruiting additional faculty for undergraduate and graduate programs. Zephyrhills Republican Sen. Randy Maggard and Dade City Republican Rep. Jim Burgess sponsored the budget requests. The town's $995,000 will support stormwater improvements for the proposed St. Leo Town Center, a mixed-use development envisioned as a central gathering place for residents, visitors and the university.

cards.headline: Florida Chamber poll finds 64% of state voters very proud to be American during 250th anniversary
cards.teaser: A statewide Florida Chamber of Commerce poll shows most Floridians are proud to be Americans during the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, though responses fall along partisan and age lines.
cards.body:
A statewide poll conducted by the Florida Chamber of Commerce shows 64% of Floridians say they are "very proud" to be American during the 250th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Another 12% say they are "somewhat proud," while 12% indicate they are not proud at all. The survey of 604 likely voters was conducted between May 1 and May 9. Mark Wilson, President and CEO of the Florida Chamber of Commerce, said the poll demonstrates that Floridians take pride in the nation, in Florida's national leadership, and in the entrepreneurial spirit that defines America.

Perceptions of American pride fall sharply along partisan lines. Some 89% of Republicans say they are very proud Americans compared to 34% of Democrats, while 58% of no-party voters say the same. About 25% of Democrats say they're not proud at all of being American, compared to only 2% of Republicans and 12% of no-party voters. Age also significantly influenced responses, with 71% of Floridians over 60 saying they're very proud to be American versus just 42% of those under 40. On American history broadly, 74% of Florida voters say Americans should be proud of the nation's history, with only 12% saying they feel ashamed. Republicans led at 91% on this question compared to 51% of Democrats and 71% of no-party voters.

cards.headline: U.S. Sugar deploys autonomous tractors in largest commercial rollout in American sugar industry
cards.teaser: U.S. Sugar announced the deployment of five autonomous tractors in its Clewiston operations, marking what the company calls the largest commercial rollout of driverless tractors in the American sugar industry.
cards.body:
U.S. Sugar has deployed five autonomous tractors in what the company calls the largest commercial rollout of autonomous tractors in the American sugar industry. The fleet includes four John Deere 8R Series tractors and one 9R Series machine, each retrofitted to operate continuously without a driver. A single technician monitors multiple machines simultaneously from a remote command center. The autonomous technology comes from Autonomous Solutions, Inc., a Utah-based company that installs its Vehicle Automation Kit onto the tractors' existing systems. Everglades Equipment Group supplied the tractors.

For worker Harman Avalos, the shift has been dramatic. After three years of driving tractors up to ten hours daily, he now monitors the same machines from an air-conditioned trailer with a laptop. Precision Agriculture Manager Scott Berden noted that modern farming is far more high-tech than most people realize, countering the common image of farmers in overalls with pitchforks. U.S. Sugar plans to eventually expand the technology across its entire 250,000-acre operation, an area stretching about 375 miles and nearly ten times the size of Miami. The feature appears in Florida Trend's July issue.

cards.headline: Arizona Senator Mark Kelly endorses Democrats challenging Mills, Bilirakis in Florida congressional races
cards.teaser: Arizona Senator Mark Kelly threw his support to two Democrats with military backgrounds running to flip Florida congressional seats, backing Bale Dalton and Darren McAuley.
cards.body:
Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain and former astronaut, endorsed two Florida Democrats challenging Republican incumbents. Kelly announced his support during a social media event backing 10 Democrats with military backgrounds running for Congress. "Veterans understand what it means to put country before self," Kelly posted. "These leaders did it during their time in service, and now they're answering the call again to fight for their communities in Congress."

Bale Dalton, a former Navy helicopter pilot and NASA Chief of Staff who served 24 years in the Navy and Navy Reserve, is challenging Rep. Cory Mills in Florida's 7th Congressional District. Dalton was recently named to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's Red to Blue program. Kelly praised Dalton's qualifications to "put people over politics and deliver results for Florida families who are struggling to get by." In Florida's 12th Congressional District, Darren McAuley, a former Veterans Affairs physician and Florida's State Air Surgeon, is running against 20-year incumbent Rep. Gus Bilirakis, a Palm Harbor Republican. Kelly said McAuley "has spent his life helping others, including fellow service members and veterans" and is "running to be the fighter families in FL-12 need." Both candidates welcomed Kelly's endorsement.

hero.headline: Martin County free clinic sees surge in patients after ACA subsidies expire, has capacity for more
hero.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is experiencing increased patient volume following the expiration of enhanced federal subsidies under the Affordable Care Act at the beginning of the year. The clinic has announced it has capacity to serve additional patients who have lost health insurance coverage as a result of the subsidy changes.

While only about 20 patients have sought care at Volunteers in Medicine after losing coverage, estimates suggest upwards of 500 Martin County residents may have lost access to health insurance. Bromberg emphasized the importance of early medical screening, noting that "there are a lot of things that get screened for that if they're found early can prevent terrible outcomes." He stressed that the clinic has room for many more patients and encouraged those who need care to reach out.

Rokaya McGarry represents one of the many residents affected by the subsidy expiration. After the enhanced financial assistance ended, she could no longer afford health insurance. McGarry fell seriously ill following the loss of her mother, developing bronchitis and feeling weak. In desperation, she called Volunteers in Medicine and was seen by the clinic within a day. She initially viewed medical care as a luxury until her health crisis forced her to seek help. McGarry expressed her gratitude for the clinic's assistance, saying "I can't even express how grateful I am to them because I don't know where I'd be."

The clinic provides free medical care with no eligibility restrictions attached to the service. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must have an annual income under $39,990, or families of four must earn less than $82,500 per year. Bromberg emphasized that many more people in the community could benefit from the clinic's services and encouraged those who have lost coverage to contact them. The clinic's outreach efforts highlight a critical gap in healthcare access for low-income residents in the region.

Both methamphetamine and MDMA are controlled substances with significant legal consequences when found in trafficking quantities. Under Florida law, the possession of these substances in amounts exceeding certain thresholds automatically elevates charges to trafficking level, which carries much more severe penalties than simple possession. The 100-plus grams seized in this case clearly met that threshold.

This arrest is part of ongoing drug enforcement efforts by law enforcement in the Fort Pierce area. cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach, a roadway that residents say has flooded regularly during both heavy and light storms. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. State Sen. Mack Bernard said securing the funding was a major step forward after DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million only covers a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost.

Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans for improvements three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to accommodate larger underground drainage pipes designed to reduce flooding. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029. Residents have described water pushing into driveways and leaving debris scattered across properties after storms, with some calling the flooding severe enough to warrant a nickname: "Lake Australian Avenue."
